title: The goal
question: I want to generate text.
explanation: Instead of writing a whole sentence at once, I can grow it one small piece at a time. I start with some text, add a piece, then repeat.
caption: This is an illustration of growing text, not output from a running model.
next: To choose what to add, I need a way to guess what comes next.

title: The next guess
question: I need to guess the next character.
explanation: After “ca”, I might see “t”, “r”, or “n”. There is no single right answer for every situation. I need probabilities: numbers that say how likely each choice is.
caption: The possibilities depend on the text the model has seen.
next: First, I need to decide exactly what kind of piece I am predicting.

title: Tokens
question: I need to split text into pieces.
explanation: A token is one piece of text the model handles at a time. For our first model, each character is a token, including spaces. Larger language models often use pieces of words instead.
caption: Here, three characters make three tokens. We keep this rule for the rest of the journey.
next: Now I need a consistent way to identify each token in my calculations.

title: Token IDs
question: I give each token a number.
explanation: I make a vocabulary: a list of the tokens my model knows. Each gets a token ID, like a numbered seat. That lets me use it to look up counts and, later, learned numbers. The ID is a label, not a meaning or a score.
caption: We could renumber the vocabulary, as long as all our lookups stayed consistent.
next: With tokens identified, I can count which ones tend to follow each other.

title: A working first model
question: Counts already let me complete “ca”.
explanation: My tiny collection contains “cat” six times, “car” three times, and “can” once. After “a”, I count the next characters and divide by ten. I can now complete “ca” by choosing “t” 60% of the time, “r” 30%, and “n” 10%. No embeddings are needed for this model.
caption: For this first exercise, we stop after completing the three-letter word. The count model only looks at the last character.
next: This solves our tiny task. To move toward a larger neural model, I want to reuse what it learns instead of storing every transition independently.

title: Separate entries
question: A separate entry for every pair gets expensive.
explanation: A direct table can store one adjustable score for every input token and possible next token. A score says how much to favor that output; it is not yet a probability. Our five tokens need only 5 × 5 = 25 entries. With 10,000 tokens, that becomes 100 million. Can I build scores from fewer, shared ingredients?

example.label: The row we care about now
example.value: input “a” → scores for t, r, n

caption: This is a reason to explore a different representation, not a claim that our five-token problem needs compression. A table of counts remains a valid solution.
next: I will try making each row from a small number of reusable scoring patterns.

title: Reusable patterns
question: A weight controls one contribution.
explanation: Suppose I use two shared patterns of output scores. Pattern A favors “t”; pattern B favors “n”. I can multiply each pattern by a number, called a weight, to control its contribution. For the input “a”, I will try 0.75 of A and 0.25 of B.
caption: These patterns and settings are invented to explain the calculation. They are not probabilities and have not been fitted to our counts. We show three output columns; a complete model also has columns for c and a.
next: I need to keep those two settings together, in a fixed order.

title: Keep the settings together
question: The vector holds the recipe for a prediction.
explanation: For “a”, I store [0.75, 0.25]: first the amount of pattern A, then the amount of pattern B. This ordered list is a vector. Its job here is precise: it tells the shared calculation how much of each pattern to use. It is not just a new number identifying “a”.
caption: A vector is simply an ordered list. Here its entries control contributions to scores; unlike probabilities, such settings may be negative and need not sum to one.
next: Why not use just one setting? Because I want to adjust the two patterns independently.

title: Independent settings
question: Two entries let the recipe change in two ways.
explanation: With only one multiplier on pattern A, I could make its scores bigger or smaller, but could not turn it into pattern B. Two independent settings let me move between these patterns and combine them. Each setting is a dimension of the vector.
caption: Two settings still cannot produce every possible score row. This smaller model trades flexibility for shared structure. More dimensions allow more patterns.
next: Different input tokens need different recipes. I will keep their vectors in a table.

title: Look up the recipe
question: An embedding is the recipe stored for a token.
explanation: I give every input token its own vector of settings. This lookup table is the embedding table. The ID of “a” selects its row, [0.75, 0.25]. Every prediction that uses “a” can reuse that same row. Training will adjust the rows and the shared scoring patterns together.
caption: The ID finds the recipe; the embedding contains its adjustable settings. Real embedding dimensions are not assigned labels like “catness” by hand. Our A/B patterns only make their computational role visible.
next: This changes how many numbers we store: a short recipe per token, plus shared patterns for turning recipes into scores.

title: What this buys us
question: Reuse calculations instead of learning every pair separately.
explanation: For our five-token vocabulary, a two-entry embedding for each input needs 10 numbers. Two shared patterns across five possible outputs need another 10. That is 20 numbers instead of 25 independent scores. Updating a shared pattern affects every input that uses it, so training examples can influence a common calculation.
caption: The saving is small here and larger for bigger vocabularies with short vectors. Fewer numbers do not guarantee better predictions; a two-pattern model cannot match every possible table. A transformer adds further calculations on these vectors.
next: Now let’s actually use the embedding of “a” to calculate the three scores for completing “ca”.

title: Make one score
question: Follow the recipe for “t”.
explanation: The embedding of “a” is [0.75, 0.25]. In the “t” column, pattern A contains 2 and pattern B contains 0. Multiply each setting by its matching pattern value, then add. The result is the score for “t”. This multiply-and-add operation is a weighted sum.
caption: The output values 2 and 0 are adjustable weights too. “Weight” means a multiplier in the calculation, not confidence or probability.
next: Repeat the same calculation for “r” and “n”, using their columns in the same shared patterns.

title: Make all scores
question: One recipe produces all three scores.
explanation: Keep the embedding [0.75, 0.25] fixed. Only the output column changes. This produces a list of scores for “t”, “r”, and “n”. The shared pattern table is a matrix; matrix multiplication carries out these weighted sums together.
caption: The embedding represents the input “a”. This new vector represents output scores. Both are lists, but their positions have different jobs.
next: To choose a character, I need probabilities rather than raw scores.

title: Scores to chances
question: Convert the scores into chances of being chosen.
explanation: Softmax turns scores into positive probabilities that add up to one. It gives higher scores a larger share. Applied to our three scores, it produces about 50.6% for “t”, 30.7% for “r”, and 18.6% for “n”. That is a prediction for the same “ca” we started with.
caption: The rounding makes the displayed percentages total 99.9%. Softmax exponentiates each score, then divides by the sum. This demonstration considers only t/r/n; a full vocabulary distribution includes c/a too.
next: Our invented settings do not match the observed proportions yet. Training is how we make them more useful.

title: Practice examples
question: The text supplies the answer to practice with.
explanation: I present “cat”, “car”, and “can” with their observed frequencies: six, three, and one. For each example, I give the model “ca” and ask it to predict the final token. The real final token supplies the answer for that training example.
caption: Our simple neural model currently uses the final input token “a”. Many examples teach it a distribution, rather than a rule that always chooses “t”.
next: I need a single number that says how poorly this prediction matched the observed token.

title: Measure the mistake
question: Loss measures how much improvement is needed.
explanation: For next-token prediction, the loss gets smaller when the model assigns more probability to the token that actually occurred. Being very confident in a wrong answer gives a large loss. Combining losses across many examples gives training something concrete to reduce.
caption: The usual calculation is negative log probability. You do not need that formula to see the aim: increase probability for the observed outcomes across the training examples.
next: The loss tells me how bad the prediction was. It does not yet tell me which number to change.

title: Find a direction
question: Ask what a small change would do.
explanation: For each adjustable number, I need to know whether increasing it slightly would raise or lower the loss. A derivative describes this local effect. Collecting these derivatives gives a gradient. Backpropagation calculates them by tracing how the loss depends on the earlier calculations.

example.label: Positive derivative
example.value: A small increase would raise loss.

example.label: Negative derivative
example.value: A small increase would lower loss.

caption: These are local directions, not promises about a large change. We can let an automatic differentiation tool calculate them.
next: Now I can take a small step in a direction that should reduce the loss.

title: Small updates
question: Change the numbers a little, then try again.
explanation: An optimizer uses the gradients to update embeddings and weights. In simple gradient descent, I subtract a small multiple of each derivative from its corresponding number. The learning rate controls how big that step is. Then I make new predictions and repeat.

example.label: Suppose its derivative is 0.2; step size 0.1

caption: This derivative is hypothetical, not computed from the earlier example. Training adjusts embeddings and shared output weights together. Large steps can make things worse.
next: Our model can now learn next-character patterns. Longer text creates another problem: the most recent character alone is not enough.

title: Longer context
question: What if “cat”, “car”, and “can” appear in sentences?
explanation: Now imagine extending the training text with sentences: “the cat is sleeping”, “the car is moving”, and “the can is empty”. All three prefixes end in “is ”. A last-character model sees only the same space and must give the same prediction. Even the last word is identical. I need information from earlier tokens to distinguish the prefixes.
caption: These sentences extend our original toy collection. They illustrate why context matters; the original three-word collection could not teach these continuations.
next: The token embeddings give me vectors for the characters. I now need to preserve their order and combine information from earlier positions.

title: Keep the order
question: The same tokens can occur in a different order.
explanation: Even “cat” and “act” contain the same three characters. Their token embeddings are the same rows, arranged differently. Position information tells the context calculation which came first, second, and third.
caption: This rearrangement illustrates order, not a new training dataset. A model that simply added all token vectors would lose this distinction.
next: Attention lets the current position take different amounts of information from earlier positions.

title: Attention
question: Mix information in different proportions.
explanation: To complete “the cat is ”, the model can combine information from the earlier characters instead of using only the final space. Attention calculates how much each available position contributes, then mixes their vectors. These mixing shares change with the input. They are calculated using learned comparisons, rather than stored as one fixed recipe for every sentence.

example.label: Two illustrative transformed vectors from earlier positions

caption: These vectors and shares are invented to show the mixing operation, not learned results for our sentences. During training, future positions are hidden so the model cannot read the answer ahead.
next: The resulting vector now depends on the context. Later calculations turn it into output scores and probabilities, just as before. These added calculations must also be trained on suitable text.

title: Try new text
question: Good practice scores are not enough.
explanation: A low loss on our ten familiar words only tells me the model fits those examples. To see whether it learned useful patterns, I need a larger collection and some text kept out of training. I compare its predictions with the actual next tokens there too.

example.label: Validation text
example.value: Used to check progress, not to compute training updates.

caption: For a final evaluation, keep another test set untouched while choosing the model and settings.
next: Once I am ready to generate, I keep the learned numbers fixed.

title: Generate
question: I choose a token, then do it again.
explanation: The trained model gives me probabilities for the next token. I sample one: a more likely token has a greater chance of being chosen. I add it to the text and predict again using the updated context. Repeating this loop generates text.
caption: The text changes during generation; the trained weights stay fixed. A small model may produce nonsense—it has learned patterns, not guaranteed facts.
next: The loop is complete: identify tokens, look up vectors, combine them using weights and context, predict probabilities, and sample the next token. Practice improves the numbers behind those calculations.
